articles.summary: Una guía práctica para médicos que abren su primera oficina Por Nerma Albertorio Barnés, Abriste tu primera oficina. Ya pasaste por el financiamiento, la búsqueda de espacio, la compra de equipo; quizás contrataste a tu primer empleado. Y ahora llega la parte que incomoda a la mayoría de los médicos: darse a conocer. Es común llegar a este punto con una contradicción que no se explica en la escuela de medicina: sabes que necesitas pacientes para sostener la práctica, pero sientes que “hacer marketing ” no se ajusta a la seriedad de tu profesión. Como si promocionarte fuera lo contrario de ser un buen médico. No lo es. Lo que sí es cierto es que el marketing en salud tiene reglas distintas a las de cualquier otro negocio., Conocerlas de entrada te ahorra problemas éticos, legales y de reputación, justo cuando más necesitas que tu nombre se asocie con confianza, no con dudas. Existe una razón práctica para no ignorarlo: el mismo estudio de mercado que te llevó a solicitar financiamiento para tu primera oficina te dice que en tu zona hay pacientes que hoy están con otro médico o sin ninguno, simplemente porque no saben que existe tu oficina médica. Esperar a que “te encuentren por su cuenta” no es prudencia profesional; es dejar dinero, y pacientes que necesitan cuidado, sobre la mesa. Marketing no es venderse, es ser encontrado Piensa en esto: la persona que necesita un médico no busca publicidad. Está buscando información confiable, justo en el momento en que la necesita. Tu trabajo no es convencer a nadie de que te necesita; eso ni es ético ni es tu rol. Tu trabajo es asegurarte de que cuando alguien te necesite, te encuentre, entienda con claridad qué haces y confíe en que puede llegar a tu oficina sin fricción. En pocas palabras, la diferencia es esta: · Marketing tradicional: Crea deseo por algo que la persona no sabía que quería · Marketing en salud: Reduce la brecha entre una necesidad existente y tu oficina Eso se logra con claridad, no con persuasión agresiva. Y ahí está la clave de todo lo que sigue: si tu estrategia depende de exagerar, de generar urgencia falsa o de prometer más de lo que puedes garantizar, ya rompiste la regla más importante antes incluso de pensar en la ética profesional. Las líneas que no se deben cruzan El Código de Ética Profesional del Tribunal Examinador de Médicos de Puerto Rico no habla de Instagram ni de Google Ads; es un documento pensado para otra época, pero sus principios aplican directamente a cualquier canal que uses hoy. Tres cánones en particular que deberías tener bien presentes: · Canon 23 — No puedes anunciarte ni practicar como “especialista” en un área si no tienes la certificación correspondiente. Un fellowship informal, años de experiencia práctica o dominio de un tema no te da derecho a usar esa palabra en público sin una certificación oficial. · Canon 24 — No puedes pagar ni recibir comisión, bono o compensación de ningún tipo por el referido de pacientes ni por el endoso de un tratamiento en particular. Los “programas de referidos con incentivo”, tan comunes en otros negocios, son, en medicina, una violación directa. · Canon 16 — Todo lo que comuniques sobre tus resultados, tu experiencia o tus casos debe ser verificable personalmente. Nada de “hemos ayudado a cientos de pacientes con X” si no tienes cómo sustentarlo. A esto le sumo dos zonas grises que veo con frecuencia en consultorios nuevos: · Testimonios de pacientes. No es ilegal usarlos, pero hay que tener prudencia. Necesitas un consentimiento informado y por escrito, específico para uso público, no el general que firman para el tratamiento . Y nunca compartas fotos de “antes y después” sin un protocolo de consentimiento separado y claro sobre dónde y cómo se va a usar esa imagen. · Promesas de resultado. Hay una enorme diferencia entre “ofrecemos tratamiento para X condición” y “vamos a resolver tu problema.” La primera es información. La segunda es una promesa que no puedes garantizar y que, si no se cumple, erosiona la confianza en todo el sistema, no solo en ti. Antes de publicar algo, hazte estas tres preguntas: ¿Puedo sustentar esto con algo que yo mismo haya verificado? ¿Tengo el consentimiento explícito y por escrito de este paciente para contar su historia o mostrar su imagen? ¿Esto construye confianza a largo plazo o solo busca una venta rápida? Lo que sí funciona — y es completamente ético Con esos límites claros, hay mucho margen para crecer bien. Esto es lo que puede mover la aguja para una oficina nueva: Tu perfil de Google Business, bien hecho. La mayoría de tus primeros pacientes te van a encontrar buscando “[tu especialidad] cerca de mí” en Google, no en redes sociales. Configura tu perfil con la dirección exacta, horario actualizado, fotos reales de tu oficina, sin imágenes genéricas (Google se da cuenta) y la lista de planes médicos que aceptas. En 2026, esto no es un extra; es la puerta de entrada para que te encuentren. Contenido educativo, no promocional. En redes sociales, en lugar de publicar ofertas o “promos”, que además pueden rozar lo antiético según el contexto, comparte información útil: qué esperar en una primera cita, cómo prepararse para un examen, señales de cuándo buscar ayuda. Esto construye autoridad sin necesidad de vender nada y es exactamente el tipo de contenido que un paciente potencial comparte con su familia cuando alguien pregunta “¿Conoces un buen médico para esto?” Referidos genuinos, no pagados. La forma más efectiva y ética de crecer en medicina sigue siendo el buen servicio que se presta por sí solo, más las relaciones con otros profesionales de la salud de tu zona. Invierte tiempo en presentarte ante ellos, en dar seguimiento cuando refieres a un paciente, en ser la persona que responde cuando otro colega necesita una segunda opinión. Esas relaciones, cultivadas sin transacción de por medio, valen más que cualquier campaña pagada. Elimina la fricción en el primer contacto. Muchas oficinas nuevas pierden pacientes potenciales no por falta de marketing , sino porque resulta difícil agendar una cita. Un número de WhatsApp Business que alguien revisa a diario, un sistema simple de citas en línea y una persona que contesta el teléfono en horario laboral: eso genera los resultados que buscas, que te agenden una cita. Constancia sobre intensidad. No necesitas estar en cinco redes sociales ni publicar todos los días. Escoge un canal, como tu perfil de Google Business, Instagram o Facebook, y sé constante durante meses, no solo durante el lanzamiento. La oficina que publica fuerte el primer mes y desaparece en el segundo manda una señal peor que la de la que nunca publicó nada. Tu reputación es tu activo más valioso En un negocio de cuidado de la salud, la reputación no es “un activo de marketing ”; es, literalmente, el negocio. Cada decisión sobre cómo te promocionas debería pasar por un filtro simple: ¿esto construye o erosiona la confianza que un paciente necesita en mí antes de dejarme cuidar su salud? Ya diste el paso más difícil: conseguiste el financiamiento, abriste la puerta, pusiste tu nombre en un letrero. El marketing ético, bien hecho, no es una distracción de la medicina; es una extensión de la misma responsabilidad que tienes con cada paciente que atiendes: ser honesto, ser claro y no prometer lo que no puedes cumplir. Eso, a la larga, es lo que llena una sala de espera. No es la promesa más grande; es la confianza mejor construida. Y si en el camino necesitas ayuda para poner esto en práctica, desde ordenar tus finanzas hasta estructurar cómo comunicas tu nueva oficina, para eso está precisamente el acompañamiento que viene con el programa Primera Oficina Médica de Popular1. Úsalo. Una práctica sólida no se construye en soledad, y pedir ese apoyo desde el primer día no es una señal de debilidad; es la misma lógica de negocio que aplicaste para conseguir tu financiamiento. En resumen: · Sé encontrado antes de tener que convencer a nadie. · Sé honesto en cada canal, cada vez. · Sé constante, no solo visible durante el lanzamiento. articles.summary: Thanks to everyone who joined our recent webinar and kept the chat buzzing with questions! Missed the session or want to watch it again? Catch the full recording here. Below is the full Q&A from the session, answered by our panel - Tihomir Petrovic, Madhuri Vasa, Goutham Mandadi, and Sachin Vellanki. Test Automation Scope & Compatibility Can test automation cover UI-Kit or Theme/Cosmos apps? No - GenAI test automation is currently supported only for Constellation applications. What about hybrid apps (Constellation implementation layer, UI Toolkit/Theme-Cosmos built-on)? Yes - supported, provided the top-level end-user application is built on Constellation. Can I run application tests without Deployment Manager? Yes - download the full automation script bundle as a zip and run it locally or on any other CI/CD pipeline. Can custom components be tested? Not currently - automation covers out-of-the-box Pega base components; for custom components you'll need to write custom code or adapt the auto-generated test skeletons. Can we test external AI agents? No - this capability only tests the functionality of the Pega application itself. Is test automation available for Client-Managed Cloud, or only Pega Cloud? AI-assisted authoring is available on Client-Managed Cloud, but the automated execution infrastructure is currently exclusive to Pega Cloud 3. Is AI testing only available on Pega Cloud, not on-premise? Same answer as above - authoring works broadly, but automated execution is a Pega Cloud 3 capability today. Execution, Integration & Tooling Can external automation tools connect to Pega and execute our test cases? Not yet natively - tests currently run through Deployment Manager or within the Pega environment. An API endpoint for external tools to trigger API tests is on the roadmap. Is integrating with Playwright an option? Yes - Playwright is the primary engine. Generated tests use Playwright and TypeScript, and Pega Cloud provides native infrastructure to run them without needing third-party orchestrators like Jenkins or Azure DevOps. Do I need to install Playwright locally to run downloaded tests? Yes, if running locally (dependencies are provided). Not needed if running through Deployment Manager, since Pega handles the infrastructure as a service. Can Infinity '26 scripts be executed on another test bed, like Bamboo? Yes - download the test package and run it in your own orchestrator, as long as the environment is configured correctly. Is there a centralized view to monitor test execution across multiple pipelines? Today, the Application Quality dashboard in Deployment Manager shows execution trends for Pega Unit tests. Application Test execution trends are on the roadmap for early 2027. Can we reuse existing Playwright tests inside the Pega test suite / Deployment Manager? Not currently - the infrastructure supports only out-of-the-box Application Tests. Tagging and suite-management features are coming in future releases; please raise this as product feedback in the meantime. Can we configure simulations for integrations in an application test? No, this is not currently supported. GenAI & Maintenance Can AI generate tests for existing applications, not just new Blueprint apps? Yes - as long as the application is built on the Constellation architecture. Should we write explicit prompts to create pipelines in DM, or during Blueprint design? Discussed live during the session - please check the recording for the full nuance on prompt timing. How do we maintain test cases as screens, data, or flows change - can AI help? Yes - AI can update tests by reading the changes in a branch. Does regenerating a test automatically invalidate old ones, or do we handle cleanup? There's no automatic cleanup of test cases or test data today; this needs to be handled manually or via a utility activity. Do generated test artifacts (e.g., cases) get cleaned up automatically, like Pega Unit tests? Same as above - no automatic cleanup yet; manual or utility-activity-based cleanup is required. What are the known limitations and accuracy metrics of this capability? In the current release, the focus is on the case lifecycle - landing pages, external-only REST APIs, and custom components are not yet automated. Can we integrate external AI tools like Claude or OpenAI to generate tests directly in a Constellation app? Yes - tests are rules, so they can be generated using external AI tools via the Pega MCP protocol (a topic we may dedicate a future webinar to). Is Gen AI licensing required? Can we bring our own model (e.g., Claude via MCP)? Does this work on Client Cloud? Three-part answer: (1) it's part of the Gen AI bundle and requires a signed addendum; (2) yes, you can connect through Claude or another external harness and leverage Pega MCP to generate tests; (3) it's possible on Client Cloud - please confirm specifics with your account executive. Pipelines, Blueprint & Deployment What are the prerequisites for getting pipelines created? None from a manual setup standpoint - the process is fully automated for users on Pega Cloud 3 using Deployment Manager as a service. If an app is extended with a new Blueprint for another case type, how is the existing pipeline handled? Deployment Manager creates a "Version 2" of each relevant pipeline. Does Blueprint support reusing existing enterprise assets (data models, integrations, APIs) instead of generating new ones? Discussed live during the session - please see the recording for the detailed walkthrough. How do you recommend teams deliver a Blueprint-generated solution iteratively? Treat Blueprint as the app baseline/foundation - the generated implementation plan becomes the bridge into iterative delivery, rather than treating the branch as one large delivery unit. Are there plans to bring automatic pipeline creation to customers who don't use Pega Cloud? No current plans for Client-Managed Cloud or on-premise - please raise this as product feedback. DX API endpoints are configured per customer service package - how do we reconfigure tests with less effort? Discussed live during the session - please see the recording for the recommended approach. Reporting, Thresholds & Reliability How long are reports available, and can we adjust the pass threshold (e.g., accept 97%)? Configurable thresholds are on the roadmap; today a 100% pass rate is required, though privileged users can manually skip failed tasks. Service-level reports are kept for 7 days, while route-to-live evidence (screenshots/videos) remains until manually erased. What about load testing? These tests focus on application functionality and lifecycle, not load - load testing is handled separately with tools like JMeter or LoadRunner against a baseline. Is recording video/images an alternative to robotic testing? No - Playwright records execution videos and screenshots for UI testing, but robotic testing targets desktop applications specifically; they're distinct capabilities. Is "application test" the same as the former "scenario testing"? "Application test" is the new term for Constellation apps, covering both UI and API (DX API) testing. "Scenario Testing" is on a deprecation path since it doesn't support Constellation. What about headless applications (Pega as orchestrator only, no UI, heavy REST usage)? Focus on API tests and unit tests - API testing lets you functionally test REST services and connectors without a UI layer. We hit a runtime exception running application tests via Deployment Manager - should we open a support case? Yes, please open a support case. Do we need to configure authentication to run application tests? Yes - since tests rely on DX APIs, you'll need to configure OAuth authentication profiles and client credentials. Using bots for testing, especially for compliance and repetitive tasks? Discussed live during the session - please see the recording for this topic.

articles.summary: Before we get into it, the short version: AR automation can reduce DSO by addressing internal delays such as missed follow-ups, manual invoice errors, and slow cash application that contribute to billing lag. Invoices aging beyond 90 days often carry higher write-off risk, and collection rates tend to decline once accounts cross that threshold. A meaningful share of late B2B payments can stem from manual invoicing errors such as wrong amounts, missing PO numbers, or outdated contact information. Automated dunning sequences can be configured to trigger reminders at set milestones—for example, a reminder at day 31, an escalation at day 61, and a hold at day 90—so accounts do not age passively. Real-time ERP integration can update aging buckets as payments arrive, which may allow collectors to prioritize high-value, high-risk accounts more automatically. Automation can be configured to address upstream breakdowns by routing disputed charges early and triggering risk-based credit holds before balances become uncollectible. In short: automation fixes what you control Accounts receivable automation can shorten the time between invoice and cash by reducing the internal delays you actually control: tracking overdue accounts, sequencing follow-up, matching payments. Public materials from AR automation vendors suggest some adopters report lower DSO and better cash visibility, though automation can’t make customers pay faster. It removes friction in your process. It doesn’t promise a dramatic collections improvement on its own.

articles.summary: The Short Version In short: manual invoicing and slow collection follow-up leak revenue you’ve already earned. Accounts receivable automation closes that gap by making invoice delivery timely and follow-up automatic, the two recovery steps manual systems most often miss. Businesses can lose measurable income to revenue leakage. Optimizing order-to-cash is often cited as a material earnings improvement, though the size of that improvement depends on billing model and process maturity. Leakage tends to concentrate in recurring billing errors, failed payment recovery, and manual AR follow-up, not early sales steps. The contract-to-invoice gap and manual dunning cycles are two of the biggest culprits. The KPIs that move first: days sales outstanding, revenue leakage percentage, and collection cost per invoice. Finance teams often spend substantial time each week on invoice processing, overdue payment tracking, and reconciliation before automation removes those repetitive tasks. Skip full-scale AR automation if you send a handful of simple invoices each month. The setup may not justify the payoff. For recurring, usage-based, or milestone billing, leakage compounds fast. Optimized O2C can also free working capital that would otherwise sit in unpaid receivables.
articles.title: Order to Cash Automation for SaaS: Where Manual Invoicing Leaks Revenue

articles.summary: Parsing CMS AuthEnvelopedData message with maliciously crafted AEAD parameters can trigger a stack buffer overflow. A stack buffer overflow may lead to a crash, causing Denial of Service, or potentially remote code execution. When parsing CMS AuthEnvelopedData structures that use AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM, the IV (Initialization Vector) encoded in the ASN.1 parameters is copied into a fixed-size stack buffer without verifying that its length fits the destination. An attacker can supply a crafted CMS message with an oversized IV, causing a stack-based out-of-bounds write before any authentication or tag verification occurs. Applications and services that parse untrusted CMS or PKCS#7 content using AEAD ciphers (e.g., S/MIME AuthEnvelopedData with AES-GCM) are vulnerable. Because the overflow occurs prior to authentication, no valid key material is required to trigger it. While exploitability to remote code execution depends on platform and toolchain mitigations, the stack-based write primitive represents a severe risk. articles.summary: BRICS is not a group of allies, but an informal platform of 11 countries with different political systems, economic priorities and strategic interests. India and China are both major economies and trading partners with overlapping aspirations. Iran and the UAE have been launching missiles at each other for the last 2 mths. Several members are active in other regional and global initiatives as well - China in SCO and BRI, India in Quad , Brazil in G20. This diversity reflects multiple partnerships that major economies maintain today. When consensus is required among all BRICS members, outcomes tend to settle at the lowest common denominator. These include knowledge exchange, working groups, joint statements. They are useful but don't move the real economy. This happens through businesses. So, the question to ask is: does BRICS help build projects, reduce costs, deepen markets or secure supply chains? If not, it risks becoming a talking shop. The solution lies in a sparingly used model: minilateralism. Smaller groups of countries - 3-4 at a time - should move ahead in sectors where interests align. The broader BRICS framework can provide direction and legitimacy. But execution should come from coalitions of the willing. Focus must be on concrete-enough initiatives where cooperation creates economic value for all participants. Airbus emerged through structured industrial cooperation between France, Germany, Britain and Spain, with each country responsible for different parts of the value chain. Thereby, their respective national aerospace industries got real, durable manufacturing work and tech capability. International Space Station brought together the US and Russia, aligning two countries with divergent interests around a tangible project with mutual dependence built into its design. BRICS needs to take a similar approach. Three areas stand out: Critical minerals, clean-energy supply chains BRICS countries collectively possess resources, capital, manufacturing capacity and demand. Yet, much of this value remains fragmented. Minilateral coalitions could integrate value chains. Mineral-rich economies like Brazil and South Africa could partner through co-investment and long-term offtake arrangements with demand centres like India, supported by Gulf capital. The objective should be to move from exporting raw materials to producing higher-value products, while creating complementary strengths. Brazil and South Africa would capture greater value from their resources. India could serve as a manufacturing and demand hub. Gulf countries could deploy capital into long-term industrial assets. And China could contribute its scale, manufacturing expertise and experience in building clean energy ecosystems. Nuclear power & advanced energy tech IAEA estimates global nuclear capacity could more than double by 2050, while around 30 countries are exploring nuclear power. This creates a large opportunity for BRICS countries to collaborate on reactor supply chains, fuel services, engineering capabilities, and next-gen technologies like fusion. It's also where countries like Russia, China and India have similar starting capabilities and complementary strengths. Technical cooperation in clearly defined areas can reduce costs, accelerate learning and open new export opportunities. Strategic materials partnerships Coordinated strategic material stockpiles supported by New Development Bank (NDB) can be established. Member countries can work together to improve supply security through coordinated reserves of critical minerals and materials. Such arrangements would enhance resilience, while supporting industrial development across economies. BRICS' diversity should be viewed as a strength. Its purpose is not to eliminate competition among members, but to identify areas where cooperation can create additional value, investment and growth. Which is why sector-specific coalitions is the right approach. Countries that want to cooperate on batteries should do so. Those seeking to build biofuels ecosystems should move ahead. Others can collaborate on transmission networks, logistics corridors, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing or payment systems. Participation should be based on capability and interest, not forced consensus. If BRICS can become a platform that helps businesses build together, it will create a model of practical cooperation that the world increasingly needs.
articles.title: How BRICS can become a platform that helps businesses build together

(Sept. 29, 2026) — The University of Kansas Health System and Ardent Health (NYSE: ARDT) announced the signing of a definitive agreement today for The University of Kansas Health System to acquire full ownership of St. Francis Campus and affiliated care locations in Topeka, following a successful joint venture partnership of nearly 10 years. Under the new ownership structure, all operational responsibilities and clinical functions previously managed by Ardent Health since the beginning of the partnership will transition to The University of Kansas Health System, further integrating the campus into its broader health system. “As St. Francis enters this exciting new era, we will continue to focus on what matters most: expanding access to exceptional care, supporting our local workforce and improving the health of the communities we serve,” said Bob Page, CEO of The University of Kansas Health System. “This transition is aligned with our initial commitment to sustain and grow the hospital and clinics in service to future generations.” When Ardent Health and The University of Kansas Health System joined forces in 2017, St. Francis faced an uncertain future. The joint venture stabilized the campus, preserved access to care and protected jobs for the Topeka community. Since then, the partnership has expanded access to care through over 20 new clinics and outpatient care sites and the addition of advanced cardiovascular and cancer care services while earning national recognition for quality and safety. This transition marks the natural next step for St. Francis's future. “We’re proud of what this partnership has made possible for St. Francis and the Topeka community,” said Dave Caspers, president and CEO of Ardent Health. “We regularly evaluate our portfolio to ensure we’re focusing our resources where our operating model, scale and capabilities can have the greatest impact and create long-term value. This transition reflects that approach, while positioning St. Francis to become more fully integrated with Kansas’s largest academic health system. We look forward to supporting a thoughtful transition and to seeing St. Francis continue to thrive.” Upon closing the deal, to happen later this year, patients will not experience disruptions to care and will be able to continue accessing the services and providers they know and trust. Ardent Health will remain involved in daily campus operations for a period of time to be defined at deal close to ensure the continuation of existing strategic projects for the benefit of St. Francis’s patients, physicians, employees and community. Under The University of Kansas Health System’s ownership, patients will have even greater access to an extensive, statewide network of care that brings together expert academic medicine and local care. “As we move through the next phase of our transition, we look forward to gaining a deeper understanding of existing opportunities to strengthen services, expand specialties and enhance connections between St. Francis and The University of Kansas Health System while still keeping care local,” said Tammy Peterman, president and chief operating officer of The University of Kansas Health System. The transaction is subject to necessary approvals and other customary closing conditions, with both organizations expecting to complete the transition by the end of 2026. Ardent Health and The University of Kansas Health System are committed to providing patients and community members with consistent updates as this process continues. "This transition is about making sure more people across Kansas have access to the care they need, regardless of where they live," Page said. "We're committed to expanding access while maintaining the safe, compassionate, high-quality care the Topeka community has come to expect. We're excited about what this next chapter means for our patients, our employees and the future of health care in the region." About The University of Kansas Health System The University of Kansas Health System is the region's premier academic health system, providing a full range of care. The health system is affiliated with the University of Kansas Schools of Medicine, Nursing and Health Professions and their leading-edge research. In the Kansas City metro area, the health system offers more than 150 hospital and clinic locations, including a hospital in Kansas City, Kansas, hospitals in Olathe, Miami County and Liberty and two mental and behavioral health hospitals in the Kansas City area. The health system in Kansas City has received Magnet nursing designation five times in a row, and most recently was awarded Magnet with distinction. The University of Kansas Hospital has ranked every year since 2007 on U.S. News & World Report's Best Hospitals lists (best in Kansas and Kansas City). It provides the region's most experienced, nationally verified burn center and Level I Trauma Center, as well as a leading transplant program in liver, pancreas, kidney, heart and blood and marrow. The cancer program is part of The University of Kansas Cancer Center, a National Cancer Institute-designated comprehensive cancer center. In rural Kansas, the health system includes a hospital and outpatient facilities in Great Bend and are involved throughout the state via The University of Kansas Health System Care Collaborative. About Ardent Health Ardent Health (NYSE: ARDT) is a leading provider of healthcare in growing mid-sized urban communities across the U.S. The Company delivers care through its subsidiaries, which include 30 acute care hospitals and more than 280 sites of care with over 2,000 employed and affiliated providers across six states. Anchored by a shared operating model and a commitment to investing in innovative services and technologies that improve quality, access and experience, Ardent is focused on delivering strong clinical outcomes and improving the health of the patients and communities it serves.

articles.summary: India should aim to be a consumer as well as a producer electrostate, with electricity as the organising principle of economic development Many commentators have recently spoken about the idea of an “electrostate”. Some see it as a country powered by renewable energy . Others view it as a manufacturing hub for batteries, solar panels, and green hydrogen. My definition is broader. An electrostate is an economy that organises its growth model around electricity. As India pursues the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047, we need a model capable of delivering several objectives at once: faster growth, manufacturing competitiveness, technological leadership, energy security, exports, jobs, and strategic autonomy. Electricity sits at the intersection of all these goals. The next growth cycle will be far more electricity-intensive than the last. AI, data centres, electric mobility, advanced manufacturing , semiconductors, and digital infrastructure run on electricity. India must not merely consume these technologies. It should build an economy around them, and use low-cost electrification to restore cost leadership in steel, cement, aluminium, chemicals, textiles, and automotives, our foundational industries. This is not about clean energy alone, though it will naturally lead as it is the cheapest source of new power. The real idea is to make electricity the organising principle of economic development. As a consumer electrostate, we would progressively replace imported oil and gas with electricity across transport, industry, buildings and digital infrastructure. Electricity accounts for only around 21% of our final energy consumption. An electrostate vision will aim to raise it to 60% by 2047. As a producer electrostate, India would manufacture and export solar modules, batteries, power electronics, electrolysers, transmission equipment, and green hydrogen. Add to this the export of green compute, as India becomes a preferred home for data centres powering global AI. There is a $40-50 billion export opportunity. China is the only country that is a consumer as well as producer electrostate. That is the model India should replicate. It’s tempting to think electricity could do for India what oil did for West Asia. The analogy is useful, but incomplete. Oil transformed countries like Saudi Arabia and the UAE because it became the foundation of national development. Cheap domestic energy enabled energy-intensive industries such as aluminium and steel, financed infrastructure, powered exports, and built geopolitical influence. Oil enriched one sector and financed an economy. Electricity can improve the productivity and efficiency in large parts of the economy, because it enables more efficient, precise, automated, and scalable production systems. For a country of India’s scale, that distinction matters. A successful growth model cannot rest on one sector. It must create jobs, attract investment, support exports, and strengthen resilience. Making the electrostate idea real will require action on three fronts. A stronger electricity push: By 2047, India could need roughly five times today’s generation and eight times renewable capacity, so we must treble our pace of clean-power deployment. That means scaling solar, wind and storage faster, building transmission ahead of demand, and adding nuclear and other firm power. Reducing delivered cost of electricity to industry and data centres: It may be the single most important competitiveness challenge facing India, and the key driver that will push industries needing heat to shift from coal and oil to electricity. India produces some of the cheapest renewable electricity. Yet industrial consumers rarely benefit fully, since generation is only part of the bill. Between 30% and 45% of industrial electricity costs come from transmission charges, losses, duties, and cross-subsidies rather than generation itself. This higher cost flows into everything else, from food to manufactured goods, eroding productivity and investment attractiveness. China and Vietnam have engineered their systems to strip out many of these costs for industry. In sectors such as aluminium, polysilicon, chlor-alkali chemicals, electric-arc-furnace steel, and data centres where power can exceed 50% of production costs, their cheaper delivered electricity gives them a structural edge in attracting investment. India needs no tech breakthrough. We need to reform how we set tariffs, how states earn electricity revenues, how we discipline the completion of transmission lines, and how we solve right-of-way and land bottlenecks. Resilient grid: It should be able to carry electricity from and to all corners of India, with a capacity to absorb energy from millions of rooftop installations and deliver it to the biggest aluminium smelters. We need to rapidly build a grid that is larger, smarter, more flexible, and in the right geographies. Smarter combination of industrial and trade policy: We have several schemes. The task now is to link demand tools, cost competitiveness, manufacturing scale, exports, standards, and skills into one framework. In electric mobility, tighter mandates, wider charging networks, and harmonised standards do more than boost EV adoption; they create predictable demand for batteries and power electronics, encouraging long-term manufacturing investment. Our solar sector shows the same pattern: incentives, demand creation, standards, and trade measures work far better as one system than as scattered schemes. Finally, India should create Export India, modelled on Invest India, a government-backed platform offering market intelligence, buyer facilitation, standards navigation, and deal support, backed by diplomacy. Helping Indian electro-tech companies win global markets will be as important as helping them manufacture in the first place. India’s opportunity is not to merely to shift to electricity faster. It is to build something more relevant now: a producer and consumer electrostate that combines energy security, industrial competitiveness, exports, and inclusive growth into a single national mission.

articles.summary: Blueprint Onboarding & AI Test Authoring and Automation: DevOps at Speed On September 17, 2026, Pega hosted a live session - Accelerate DevOps with Blueprint Onboarding & AI-Driven Test Authoring & Automation - as part of the Pega as-a-Service Webinar Series. The panel brought together Tihomir Petrovic (Technical Solution Director, PSA Competency Center for DevOps), Madhuri Vasa (Product Manager, Deployment Manager & DevOps experiences), Goutham Mandadi (Senior Principal Software Engineer, GenAI test automation), and Sachin Vellanki (Product Owner, Automated Testing). Together they showed how Pega GenAI™ and Pega Autopilot™ are reshaping quality assurance for Constellation applications, and how Blueprint-designed apps now flow automatically into CI/CD pipelines through Deployment Manager. Missed it live? You can watch the full recording here. From Blueprint to Pipeline in Minutes Blueprint already accelerates the design phase of an application - now Deployment Manager automates the second half of the SDLC too. Blueprint-designed apps are automatically onboarded with versioned merge and deployment pipelines, pre-aligned with Blueprint delivery methodology, right out of the box. In a live demo, the team imported a "Benefit Me" application from Blueprint and watched Deployment Manager generate validated pipelines with quality gates already configured. AI-Assisted Test Authoring at Speed Starting with release '26, an AI Assistant reads a case's lifecycle, views, and data model to automatically generate Business Actions and Application Tests for entire case types - or a whole application - expressed as Gherkin/Cucumber scenarios. Goutham demonstrated this live with a single prompt, "generate application test for my home loan case types," which produced multiple realistic test scenarios for a banking app, including a loan rejection due to income. Integrated API and UI Test Generation The platform doesn't stop at one layer: it simultaneously produces API-level test steps (backed by DX APIs) and Playwright-powered UI automation scripts, both written in human-readable Cucumber syntax. That means technical and business stakeholders alike can review and understand the same test suite. Seamless Integration into Deployment Manager Pipelines Testing tasks are now native quality gates inside Deployment Manager. Teams can package and deploy tests separately from the application artifact, configure pipeline stages to trigger automated execution, and set global testing gates that every release vehicle must clear. Each run captures audited evidence - configurable screenshots, videos, and trace files - to speed up debugging. Automated Execution Across Route-to-Live Environments Tests run consistently across Development, Staging, and Production-candidate environments, catching regressions early. The demo walked through the Deployment History view, where teams can download detailed test evidence folders, and also showed a downloaded Playwright suite executed locally via npm run test. What the Audience Wanted to Know A few themes stood out in the live Q&A: native automated execution is currently exclusive to Pega Cloud via Deployment Manager as a service; testing gates today require a 100% pass rate, though configurable thresholds (e.g., 97%) are on the roadmap; AI generation currently focuses on the case lifecycle and doesn't yet cover custom components or landing pages without manual updates; and when screens or flows change in a branch, the AI Assistant can read those changes and update existing tests automatically. Keep the Conversation Going Curious about where Blueprint, Deployment Manager, and AI-driven testing are headed next? Join the Pega as-a-Service Expert Circle for access to more sessions like this one and early looks at upcoming platform capabilities. We've also published the full Q&A from this session as a separate community discussion - Q & A recap - so take a look, and if your question wasn't fully answered, drop it there and our panel will follow up.
